claim: Recent bacterial (meta)genome sequencing efforts suggest the existence of an enormous untapped reservoir of natural-product-encoding biosynthetic gene clusters in the environment.
source: Recent bacterial (meta)genome sequencing efforts suggest the existence of an enormous untapped reservoir of natural-product-encoding biosynthetic gene clusters in the environment.
evidence: This is a general statement about recent sequencing efforts and their implications, drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Large differences in domain populations are observed from all except the most proximal and biome-similar samples.
source: We see large differences in domain populations from all except the most proximal and biome-similar samples, suggesting that most microbiomes will encode largely distinct collections of bacterial secondary metabolites.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the study, specifically the Jaccard distance analyses shown in the figures.

claim: Most microbiomes will encode largely distinct collections of bacterial secondary metabolites.
source: We see large differences in domain populations from all except the most proximal and biome-similar samples, suggesting that most microbiomes will encode largely distinct collections of bacterial secondary metabolites.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed differences in domain populations between samples.

claim: There is a correlation between geographic distance and biosynthetic diversity found in soil environments.
source: Our data indicate a correlation between two factors, geographic distance and biome-type, and the biosynthetic diversity found in soil environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the pairwise Jaccard distance analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a correlation between biome-type and biosynthetic diversity found in soil environments.
source: Our data indicate a correlation between two factors, geographic distance and biome-type, and the biosynthetic diversity found in soil environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analyses of samples from different biomes shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: Hotspots of biomedically relevant biosynthetic diversity can be identified by assigning reads to known gene clusters.
source: By assigning reads to known gene clusters we identify hotspots of biomedically relevant biosynthetic diversity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the eSNaPD analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: Soil-dwelling bacteria produce many of the most important members of our pharmacy, including the majority of our antibiotics.
source: Soil-dwelling bacteria produce many of the most important members of our pharmacy, including the majority of our antibiotics as well as many of the cytotoxic compounds used in the treatment of cancers (Cragg and Newman, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cragg and Newman, 2013.

claim: Soil-dwelling bacteria produce many of the cytotoxic compounds used in the treatment of cancers.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cragg and Newman, 2013.

claim: The traditional approach for characterizing the biosynthetic potential of environmental bacteria has been to examine metabolites produced by bacteria grown in monoculture in the lab.
source: The traditional approach for characterizing the biosynthetic potential of environmental bacteria has been to examine metabolites produced by bacteria grown in monoculture in the lab.
evidence: This is a statement about established practices in the field.

claim: The traditional monoculture approach has provided access to only a small fraction of the global microbiome's biosynthetic potential.
source: However, it is now clear that this simple approach has provided access to only a small fraction of the global microbiome's biosynthetic potential (Rappe and Giovannoni, 2003; Gilbert and Dupont, 2011; Rajendhran and Gunasekaran, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In most environments uncultured bacteria outnumber their cultured counterparts by more than two orders of magnitude.
source: In most environments uncultured bacteria outnumber their cultured counterparts by more than two orders of magnitude, and among the small fraction of bacteria that has been cultured (Torsvik et al., 1990, 1998), only a small subset of gene clusters found in these organisms is generally expressed in common fermentation broths (Bentley et al., 2002; Ikeda et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Torsvik et al., 1990, 1998.

claim: Among the small fraction of bacteria that has been cultured, only a small subset of gene clusters found in these organisms is generally expressed in common fermentation broths.
source: In most environments uncultured bacteria outnumber their cultured counterparts by more than two orders of magnitude, and among the small fraction of bacteria that has been cultured (Torsvik et al., 1990, 1998), only a small subset of gene clusters found in these organisms is generally expressed in common fermentation broths (Bentley et al., 2002; Ikeda et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bentley et al., 2002 and Ikeda et al., 2003.

claim: The direct extraction and subsequent sequencing of DNA from environmental samples using metagenomic methods provides a means of seeing biosynthetic dark matter for the first time.
source: The direct extraction and subsequent sequencing of DNA from environmental samples using metagenomic methods provides a means of seeing this 'biosynthetic dark matter' for the first time.
evidence: This is an inference about the capabilities of metagenomic methods based on established knowledge.

claim: The genomic complexity of most metagenomes limits the use of shotgun-sequencing and assembly approaches.
source: Unfortunately, the genomic complexity of most metagenomes limits the use of the shotgun-sequencing and assembly approaches (Iverson et al., 2012; Howe et al., 2014) that are now routinely used to study individual microbial genomes (Donadio et al., 2007; Cimermancic et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Iverson et al., 2012 and Howe et al., 2014.

claim: The majority of bacterial secondary metabolites arise from a very small number of common biosynthetic themes.
source: Although bacterial natural products represent an amazing diversity of chemical structures, the majority of bacterial secondary metabolites, including most clinically useful microbial metabolites, arise from a very small number of common biosynthetic themes (e.g., polyketides, ribosomal peptides, non-ribosomal peptides, terpenes, etc) (Dewick, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dewick, 2002.

claim: Most clinically useful microbial metabolites arise from a very small number of common biosynthetic themes.
source: Although bacterial natural products represent an amazing diversity of chemical structures, the majority of bacterial secondary metabolites, including most clinically useful microbial metabolites, arise from a very small number of common biosynthetic themes (e.g., polyketides, ribosomal peptides, non-ribosomal peptides, terpenes, etc) (Dewick, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dewick, 2002.

claim: Degenerate primers targeting the most common biosynthetic domains provide a means to broadly study gene cluster diversity in the uncultured majority.
source: Because of the functional conservation of enzymes used by these common systems, degenerate primers targeting the most common biosynthetic domains provide a means to broadly study gene cluster diversity in the uncultured majority in a way similar to what is now regularly done for bacterial species diversity using 16S rRNA gene sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional conservation of enzymes and established methods.

claim: This study conducts the first global examination of non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) adenylation domain (AD) and polyketide synthase (PKS) ketosynthase (KS) domain biosynthetic diversity in soil environments.
source: Here we use this approach to conduct the first global examination of non-ribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) adenylation domain (AD) and polyketide synthase (PKS) ketosynthase (KS) domain biosynthetic diversity in soil environments.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty and scope of the current study.

claim: NRPS and PKS biosynthesis were chosen for exploration because the highly modular nature of these biosynthetic systems has provided a template for the production of a wide variety of gene clusters.
source: We chose to explore NRPS and PKS biosynthesis because the highly modular nature of these biosynthetic systems has provided a template for the production of a wide variety of gene clusters that give rise to a correspondingly diverse chemical repertoire, including many of the most clinically useful microbial metabolites (Cragg and Newman, 2013).
evidence: This is a rationale based on established knowledge about NRPS and PKS systems.

claim: NRPS and PKS biosynthetic systems give rise to a correspondingly diverse chemical repertoire, including many of the most clinically useful microbial metabolites.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cragg and Newman, 2013.

source: With the help of a citizen science effort (www.drugsfromdirt.org), soil samples were collected from five continents (North America, South America, Africa, Asia, Australia) and several oceanic islands (Hawaii, Dominican Republic), covering biomes that include multiple rainforests, temperate forests, deserts and coastal sediments.
evidence: This describes the sampling methodology used in the study.

claim: The collected samples cover biomes that include multiple rainforests, temperate forests, deserts and coastal sediments.
source: With the help of a citizen science effort (www.drugsfromdirt.org), soil samples were collected from five continents (North America, South America, Africa, Asia, Australia) and several oceanic islands (Hawaii, Dominican Republic), covering biomes that include multiple rainforests, temperate forests, deserts and coastal sediments.
evidence: This describes the diversity of biomes sampled in the study.

claim: DNA was extracted directly from soils as previously described.
source: DNA was extracted directly from these soils as previously described (Brady, 2007) and 96 samples were chosen for analysis of NRPS/PKS diversity using 454 pyro-sequencing of AD and KS domain PCR amplicons.
evidence: This describes the methodology with a citation to a previous protocol.

claim: 96 samples were chosen for analysis of NRPS/PKS diversity using 454 pyro-sequencing of AD and KS domain PCR amplicons.
source: DNA was extracted directly from these soils as previously described (Brady, 2007) and 96 samples were chosen for analysis of NRPS/PKS diversity using 454 pyro-sequencing of AD and KS domain PCR amplicons.

claim: Samples were chosen on the basis of DNA quality and biome diversity.
source: Samples were chosen on the basis of DNA quality and biome diversity; raw sequence reads from these samples were combined with existing amplicon datasets derived from other biomes using the same DNA isolation, PCR and sequencing protocols (Charlop-Powers et al., 2014).

claim: Raw sequence reads from the 96 samples were combined with existing amplicon datasets derived from other biomes using the same DNA isolation, PCR and sequencing protocols.
source: Samples were chosen on the basis of DNA quality and biome diversity; raw sequence reads from these samples were combined with existing amplicon datasets derived from other biomes using the same DNA isolation, PCR and sequencing protocols (Charlop-Powers et al., 2014).

claim: The entire dataset represents 185 biomes.
source: The entire dataset representing 185 biomes was clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at a sequence distance of 5%.
evidence: This describes the scope of the final dataset.

claim: The dataset was clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at a sequence distance of 5%.
source: The entire dataset representing 185 biomes was clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at a sequence distance of 5%.

claim: Millions of unique sequencing reads yielded a predicted Chao1 OTU estimate of greater than 350,000 for each domain.

claim: Rarefaction analysis suggests that the sequence space of either domain has not yet been saturated.

claim: Most Jaccard distances between samples were found to be quite small (<3%), indicating large differences in secondary metabolite gene sequence composition between almost all sample collection sites.
source: Most Jaccard distances were found to be quite small (<3%), indicating large differences in secondary metabolite gene sequence composition between almost all sample collection sites (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Jaccard distance analysis shown in Figure 1B,D.

claim: On a global level, the strongest biosynthetic sequence composition relationships are seen between samples collected in close physical proximity to one another.
source: On a global level, the strongest biosynthetic sequence composition relationships are seen between samples collected in close physical proximity to one another (Figure 1B,D,E,F) as opposed to between samples from similar biomes in different geographic locations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analyses shown in Figure 1B,D,E,F.

claim: The strongest biosynthetic sequence composition relationships are not seen between samples from similar biomes in different geographic locations.
source: On a global level, the strongest biosynthetic sequence composition relationships are seen between samples collected in close physical proximity to one another (Figure 1B,D,E,F) as opposed to between samples from similar biomes in different geographic locations.
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the data analysis.

claim: At a cutoff of 3% shared KS or AD OTUs, essentially all inter-sample relationships are observed between immediate geographic neighbors and not similar biomes in different global locations.
source: For example, at a cutoff of even as low as 3% shared KS or AD OTUs, essentially all inter-sample relationships are observed between immediate geographic neighbors and not similar biomes in different global locations (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the network analysis shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Limited inter-sample relationships are observed between samples from the Eastern hemisphere because most samples from this part of the world were collected from sites at a significant geographic distance from one another.
source: This likely explains the limited inter-sample relationships we observe between samples from the Eastern hemisphere as most samples from this part of the world were collected from sites at a significant geographic distance from one another.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the observed pattern in the data.

claim: Soil samples from South Africa exhibit similar pairwise Jaccard metrics to those observed between geographically proximal samples collected in the Western hemisphere.
source: The only exception is the set of soil samples from South Africa, of which a number were collected in relatively close geographic proximity. These samples exhibit similar pairwise Jaccard metrics to those observed between geographically proximal samples collected in the Western hemisphere (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the Jaccard distance analysis shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Change in the biome type is an important additional factor for the differentiation of biosynthetic diversity on a more local level.
source: Although differences in biosynthetic composition of microbiomes appear to depend at least in part on the geographic distance between samples, our data suggests that change in the biome type is an important additional factor for the differentiation of biosynthetic diversity on a more local level (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the examples shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: When the cutoff is raised to 10% shared OTUs, relationships are only seen between nearby samples belonging to the same biome.
source: For example, at a cutoff of 3% shared OTUs, essentially all inter-sample relationships are observed between immediate geographic neighbors; when this is raised to 10% shared OTUs (Figure 1E,F), relationships are only seen between nearby samples belonging to the same biome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the network analysis shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Brazilian soils collected from Atlantic rainforest, saline or cerrado sites located only a few miles from one another are distinct from other globally distributed samples.
source: In the first example, Brazilian soils were collected from Atlantic rainforest, saline or cerrado (savanna-like) sites located only a few miles from one another. Our AD and KS data show these sample are (i) distinct from other globally distributed samples, (ii) most strongly related to the samples from the same Brazilian biome and (iii) only distantly related to the samples from other Brazilian biomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: PCR-based data suggest that both geography and ecology play a role in determining the major biosynthetic components of a microbiome.
source: Although it is possible that at a much greater sampling depth all AD and KS domains will be found at all sites as predicted by Baas-Becking's 'everything is everywhere but the environment selects' hypothesis of global microbial distribution (O'Malley, 2007; de Wit and Bouvier, 2006), our PCR-based data suggest that both geography and ecology play a role in determining the major biosynthetic components of a microbiome.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PCR-based data presented in the study.

claim: The vast majority of AD and KS domain sequences coming from environmental DNA are only distantly related to functionally characterized NRP/PK gene clusters.
source: The vast majority of AD and KS domain sequences coming from environmental DNA (eDNA) are only distantly related to functionally characterized NRP/PK gene clusters, precluding precise predictions about the specific natural products encoded by the gene clusters from which most amplicons arise.
evidence: This is an observation from the sequence analysis.

claim: The distant relationship of most eDNA sequences to characterized gene clusters precludes precise predictions about the specific natural products encoded by the gene clusters from which most amplicons arise.

claim: In cases where eDNA sequence tags show high sequence similarity to domains found in functionally characterized gene clusters, this information can be used to predict the presence of specific gene cluster families within a specific microbiome.
source: However, in cases where eDNA sequence tags show high sequence similarity to domains found in functionally characterized gene clusters, this information can be used to predict the presence of specific gene cluster families within a specific microbiome.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis is the basis of the eSNaPD program, a BLAST-based algorithm for classifying the gene cluster families that are associated with eDNA-derived sequence tags.
source: This type of phylogenetic analysis is the basis of the recently developed eSNaPD program, a BLAST-based algorithm for classifying the gene cluster families that are associated with eDNA-derived sequence tags (Owen et al., 2013; Reddy et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the eSNaPD program with supporting citations.

claim: When an eDNA sequence tag clades with, but is not identical to, a reference sequence in an eSNaPD-type analysis, it is considered to be indicative of the presence of a gene cluster that encodes a congener of the metabolite encoded by the reference cluster.
source: When an eDNA sequence tag clades with, but is not identical to, a reference sequence in an eSNaPD-type analysis, it is considered to be indicative of the presence of a gene cluster that encodes a congener (i.e., a derivative) of the metabolite encoded by the reference cluster.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of eSNaPD results.

claim: eSNaPD analysis of the data from all sites reveals two distinct types of biomedically relevant natural product gene cluster 'hot spots'.
source: Interestingly, eSNaPD analysis of the data from all sites reveals two distinct types of biomedically relevant natural product gene cluster 'hot spots' within our data (Figure 2A,B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the hotspot analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The two types of hotspots include 'specific gene cluster hotspots' and 'gene cluster family hotspots'.
source: These include 'specific gene cluster hotspots' and 'gene cluster family hotspots'.
evidence: This describes the two categories of hotspots identified in the analysis.

claim: Metagenomes from 'specific gene cluster hotspots' are predicted to be enriched for a gene cluster that encodes a congener of the target natural product.
source: Metagenomes from 'specific gene cluster hotspots' are predicted to be enriched for a gene cluster that encodes a congener of the target natural product, while metagenomes from 'gene cluster family hotspots' are predicted to encode multiple congeners related to the target natural product.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the eSNaPD analysis.

claim: Metagenomes from 'gene cluster family hotspots' are predicted to encode multiple congeners related to the target natural product.

evidence: This is a prediction based on the eSNaPD analysis.

claim: Figure 2A shows several of the strongest examples of 'specific gene cluster hotspots' where reads falling into an OTU related to a specific biomedically relevant gene cluster or gene cluster family are disproportionately represented in the sequence data from individual microbiomes.

claim: Hotspots are either local in nature, consisting of only one or two samples containing sequence reads mapping to the target (epoxomycin, oocydin); regional (tiacumicinB); or global with punctuated increases in diversity (glycopeptides).
source: These examples highlight the different enrichment patterns that we observe in the environment—hotspots are either local in nature, consisting of only one or two samples containing sequence reads mapping to the target (epoxomycin, oocydin); regional (tiacumicinB); or global with punctuated increases in diversity (glycopeptides).
evidence: This describes the different patterns of hotspots observed in Figure 2A.

claim: 'Specific gene cluster hotspots' are predicted to be naturally enriched for bacteria that encode congeners of the biomedically relevant target metabolites.
source: We would predict 'specific gene cluster hotspots' (Figure 2D) are naturally enriched for bacteria that encode congeners of the biomedically relevant target metabolites, thereby potentially simplifying the discovery of new congeners.

claim: 'Specific gene cluster hotspots' potentially simplify the discovery of new congeners.

claim: Figure 2B shows examples of 'gene cluster family hotspots', where metagenomes having a disproportionately high number of OTUs mapping to a specific biomedically relevant target molecule family are highlighted.
